utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There is one preliminary matter but we can deal with that when the enters the courtroom. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours, and our first witness this morning is Milos Milincic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then while we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom I briefly deal with P6549 which was MFI'd with Witness Dragan Lalovic, 2nd of June of this year, and was used again with Witness Ratomir Maksimovic, October 15th of this year, and it was MFI'd pending a final revised translation. The revised translation has been uploaded into e-court, as we understand, under doc ID 0438-6958-A-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you're instructed to replace the current translation with the revised version of which I just mentioned the number. And the P6549 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, as always, within 48 hours if there are any problems with the translation and then we may revisit the matter if need be. Good morning, Mr. Milincic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. My I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milincic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could I please ask you to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Milos Milincic. A retired teacher of Serbo-Croatian language and literature. I was the president of the municipality of Srbac, for seven years director of the educational institute in Banja Luka, and I was retired, as I said, as a teacher of the Serbo-Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Test, test. If we could have a look at 1D1726 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise, first, the signature on this first page of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is my original signature, and it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now turn to the last page in the Serb original, do you recognise whose signature appears on this page of this written statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is, again, my signature, and the date is 12th July 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, after signing this statement did you have occasion to review the same in your own language to see if everything is correct therein?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I checked it, and I discovered a terminological error. I corrected a date, whereas everything else was accurate and fair, and I signed it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to paragraph 23 to be found on page 6 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mention that you corrected a date. In paragraph 23, what correction is necessary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: My encounter with General Mladic in Banja Luka was before the date stated herein, in August of 1992, and not as it says here. That is the correction that had to be made. In other words, the year 1992 would be the correct year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to page 4 in both languages, and I'd like to focus on paragraph 15 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this is talking about the shelling of Srbac, and it says here that you advocated that we should not respond with fire to the fire that had come from the Croatian side and it seems to indicate that no fire was returned. Is this accurate or is there a correction or clarification required?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, the real reason why I was summoned to see the general in Banja Luka two months later is what it says here; that is to say, that there was no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. It is difficult to comprehend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you should slow down. Otherwise, your words will be lost because the interpreters can not follow you at such speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat, it says here that the Srbac Brigade or, rather, we did not return fire on the Croatian side but it is true that the manpower did not fire at Davor, which is the neighbouring Croatian municipality, the aim of which had been to create a provocation from the Croatian side, believing that if they target Srbac, that the Srbac artillery would retaliate against the place called Davor which is across the river Sava. I don't know what is exactly inaccurate, but I would say that the only accurate thing is that we did not return fire, but not at Davor which was innocent, but we returned fire on the highway, somewhere in the direction of Dobrinja, I think it's called, which is in the direction of Slavonski Brod from which a lorry-mounted launcher was used as well as multi-rocket-launcher and after the attack, they pulled out under a fly-over. The escorts from Motajica mountain were able to spot the location wherefrom the fire had originated, and the artillery of Srbac did not retaliate against Davor but, rather, responded to the general area. When I say general area, I mean that the fire coming from Croatian side was disguised, and this is something that I wanted to add to item 15, which means that artillery retaliated but not against Davor but rather targeted the place of origin of fire. Later on I was reported, and some allegations were made against me, with the general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand no return fire to Davor but return fire, and you mentioned one specific target, that was this mobile launcher, and, in more general terms, to the area from where fire had come. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, apart from this -- these clarifications and corrections that we've gone through today, do you stand by everything else in your statement as written?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. In short, yes. We can go into some details, but essentially that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go into some details, sir, but recall my time is short. Could you please just answer my questions. If I were to ask you today the same questions, would your answers be the same as recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth today. Does that mean we can conclude that the answers as recorded in the statement are truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: They are accurate. But I would like to add that it's difficult for those who are trying to prove the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are your answers as recorded in the statement truthful, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: They are truthful and authentic, and if you wish we can expand. But since you have a limited amount of time, I would say that everything is contained in my statement. That's the core of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I please tender 1D01726 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from the Prosecution side. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1726 receives number D783, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, there is one associated exhibit, 1D02991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2991 receives number D784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would read the short summary of the statement for the public. Milos Milincic, a teacher by profession, was president of the Srbac municipality from 1990 to 1997. Srbac [Realtime transcript read in error "Brigade"] municipality had about 879 non-Serbs out of a population of 22.000 in the 1990s and the situation is the same today, except that the overall population is about 19.000. There was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the last signature. One year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Census, not signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ivetic reads a summary of your statement. There's no need to change anything. That's not the evidence. The evidence is your statement. It's just to inform the public, so there's no need to intervene. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There was no private or public plan to discriminate against ethnic minorities in Srbac municipality. Neither was there any ethnic cleansing. Muslims from Srbac joined the VRS and 22 of them were wounded as members of the VRS as part of the Srbac Brigade. Srbac and Croatian Davor kept peaceful relations despite Croat forces shelling Srbac on three occasions in 1992. The witness advocated that restraint be shown and fire should not be returned on Davor. General Mladic personally supported the witness in his quest for peaceful relations. And that ends the summary, and I do have some more questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I seek clarification with respect to page 7, line 7. The transcript I see Srbac Brigade municipality at about and then follows a number of non-Serbs. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be just Srbac municipality in temporary transcript page 7, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to look at paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which can be found on page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph, which goes on to the other page, you talk about non-Serbs being in the VRS and you identify 22 that were wounded. Can you tell us how many non-Serbs from Srbac municipality were in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Before I left to come to here I checked these figures, and I was told that the figure was 78 or 79, was the number, total number of non-Serbs in the VRS, whereas in the Srbac Brigade there were some 42 or 43 of which 22 were wounded and are receiving disability pensions. And that can be proven by documents. If you allow me, I would like to add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please limit yourself to answering the question. The disability pensions are in your statement. We've read that. So, therefore, would you please limit yourself to the question. The answer then being 78 or 79, the total number. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I turn to paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what the 78 or 79 relates to, because the Srbac Brigade is -- the number there is 42. Now, of what corps of what organ are the 78 and 79, if 42 are from the Srbac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding would be that they're with other brigades in the VRS, but we can ask the witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you explain for us the difference between the numbers 79 and 42. In what -- to what membership are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Army of Republika Srpska had a number of corps and brigades and not all of Srbac conscripts were in the Srbac Brigade. They were in other units, and that's what the number 78 or 79 refers to. And we heard what the number was in the Srbac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're talking about is those recruited from Srbac in the entirety of the VRS, 78, 79 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of which 42 in the Srbac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to page 6 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus on your evidence in relation to paragraphs 23 through 25 therein. Here, you are talking of your encounter with General Mladic. Now, first, can you tell us what was the event or reason which caused you to be summoned by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: People found it incomprehensible that only 1 kilometre from Srbac across the river Sava there was a Croatian town that the people of Srbac never targeted, and they established some kind of personal reasons for that, especially since Srbac had been shelled three times from the highway without us retaliating on Davor, which is within the range, and possibly these accusations came from those people who denounced me, and they were so serious that they eventually reached General Mladic who has to have a final say about who was right and who was wrong. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The rest of your meeting with General Mladic is recorded in paragraphs 23 through 25. I'd like to ask you what did General Mladic do with you after the meeting; that is, did you go home right away or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No. I was ordered to come at 9.00 and when I presented the situation to the general, and I was rather enraged that everybody else knows more about Srbac than I did or that the commander of the brigade did, and I was surprised at being interrupted by general but he was in good mood, probably after having had a breakfast, and he said don't pay attention to those fools and don't engage in direct conflict with the Croatians. Then we went to another meeting at 10.00 where there were numerous people of the Krajina leadership, various commanders, presidents of municipalities, who were debriefing us on the situation with supplies and other problems in the municipalities. When I took to the floor and said this person came to see me, this person from Srbac is doing a good job, don't meddle with the problems of Srbac. Take care of your own backyard. Nobody needs any unnecessary conflicts. There were other words exchanged and I wanted to continue in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can intervene, has been recorded in the transcript that you said this. Is it correct that you said this or that someone else said this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I informed the general, as I said earlier, and I explained to him what the problem was and -- which was not to enter into an unnecessary conflict. And he said, Now I see that you are right and I understand what they're accusing of. Don't pay attention to those fools. And when they are thrashed, they are asking where are the red soldiers, and there's no need for you to fight with the Croats. And he reiterated that at the meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last word that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last word that you just said.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: What he told me, that I was right, he repeated the same before 500 people at another meeting, that people in Srbac are doing well, that they are not provoking any conflicts, that they are providing clothing and food for the army, and that they are keeping everything under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so that we can have a complete picture, sir, you earlier said that someone said: "... this person came to see me, this person from Srbac is doing a good job, don't meddle with the problems of Srbac. Take care of your own backyard. Nobody needs any unnecessary conflicts." Who said those words? Because it has not gotten into the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The general said that when we went to this joint meeting before 500 other representatives from the Krajina. When I wanted to take the floor, he was quicker so I said very little. This man spoke from the heart and he is right. You who keep saying that you know better what is going on in other people's yards should take care of your own backyards. Srbac was working well. I was supported in this way, my brigade, Srbac, unfortunately until the end of the war. We persevered and we did not have a confrontation with the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you left this meeting and -- this meeting with General Mladic and went back to Srbac, did the pressure for you to attack Davor go away or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: These people from other municipalities and other environments, they kept complaining because we were being soft on Davor, as they put it. And I would say to them you clear this up with General Mladic. He has the right information and he agreed that we should continue working in this way. So then the complaints went down. The hawks were not that loud anymore. We did not go into confrontation. I saw the mayor of Davor this summer, and he also had trouble with the Croatian side, and he was also being maligned. They were saying that he was a Chetnik, that he was co-operating with the Serb side, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic ever withdraw the support he had given you in your quest to keep the peace with Davor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: This agreement that he gave in 1992 remained valid throughout the war. He never withdrew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. MacDonald, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. MacDonald. You'll find him to your right. Mr. MacDonald is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, you testified twice before this Tribunal in the Krajisnik and Karadzic cases, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And in Krajisnik you testified about the murder of Halid Hadziselimovic by Ljubomir Stankovic. That's right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And you brought a document referring to a judgement of the Banja Luka military court with reference number IK23/92, and you said this document showed Ljubomir Stankovic being convicted for the murder of Halid Hadziselimovic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I brought this document. It was incomplete. This document was from the prison, the KP prison where he was serving his sentence. It was incomplete then. I believe that that was clarified at that point in time, but I see there is an attempt being made to multiply this further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, Witness, that reference number and that judgement refer to an entirely set of crimes, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The mentioned gentleman, if we are going to go for a chronology of events, had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the question simply was, the document you had shown which apparently contains a conviction, whether it was a conviction for the killing of Halid Hadziselimovic or whether it was for other offences. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know about the details. I know that this person was convicted for some of these incriminations and there were several of them. I cannot speak about something that I don't have before me. I would have to see what it was that I indicated. In 2005, when I was in the Krajisnik case, the municipalities gave me some paper and then it turned out to be invalid. Now was this that kind of sentence? I don't know. I'm not a court of law. I'm representative of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement in a paragraph in which you refer to this killing and nothing else, you say: "The murderer, Ljubomir Stankovic, son of Veljko, was convicted by the ruling of the Banja Luka military court number IK23/92." Is that document dealing with a conviction for this killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know whether it was that killing or -- because -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then your statement should have been corrected in 2014 when you suggested strongly that the document was. It was not the whole truth. It was apparently part of the truth. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- my thing's not working. Can I see where the document is mentioned in the statement and that it refers to it referring to this murder. It says that the murderer was convicted by ruling and that the murder and wounding of two Muslim Bosniaks at Kobasi committed by the same person who committed the previous crime. There is no document mentioned stating it's for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see -- well, let's see. Paragraph 13, third bullet point, deadly wounding of Halid Hadziselimovic, a Muslim, the murderer Ljubomir was convicted by the ruling of, and then the number follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if you read the rest of him [sic], it also mentions other crimes that this individual did. There is no reference to a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- as being specifically for this crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The document appears in the bullet point which exclusively deals with this killing and that's the reason why I said it strongly suggests. I didn't say it's untrue. I said it's not the whole of the truth. It should have said if it was about others. But apparently the witness doesn't know and that makes it even worse. He says I don't know what exactly is in there. And that should have been verified before he signed this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he is being asked about testimony from another case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- without being shown the transcript, without being shown the document, so that's why he doesn't know. We're not following the procedure of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you are telling us that what we find in this statement, that the witness has not seen this document about which he states, then, again, there may be a problem in the statement-taking practice of the Defence. He --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour. He has not been shown this statement, he has not been directed to this paragraph. So you're making allegations of what the witness is saying as to this paragraph is improper, when the Prosecution is referring to another case without showing the transcript, which is your procedure in this courtroom that you said that I have to follow, the Prosecution does not to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not at issue yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any issue, I understood the question to relate to the Hadziselimovic killing and the appearance of this number in the bullet point which exclusively deals with that killing. The witness gives a statement about this document, so the Prosecution may assume that the witness is familiar with that document without it being shown to him in court here because he comes up with it. And I leave to that at this moment. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would direct you to page 14, line 3 through 9, where this line of questioning relates to the Krajisnik case, Your Honour. I appreciate that perhaps you might recall things from that case or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But it's -- if the question is in relation to testimony in another case, the procedure is to show that testimony to the witness in court, read it, and so we're all on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd -- I understood it that the witness in this case gives the same information in his statement. That's how I understood it. But when I'm wrong, Mr. Ivetic, then I would be happy to learn that in your re-examination. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wonder, can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31607, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, can you look at this document, please. Is this the document you brought to be used in your Krajisnik testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: This is a statement of the public security station in Srbac. It is not a statement by the court. And it says very nicely what this is all about. And it says here Article 36, paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you for a moment, please. I'm just asking you to confirm if this is the document you brought in relation to the murder of Halid Hadziselimovic in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: If that is from me, if that is what I brought then, I don't remember, probably, then that's it. I don't see why all this fuss is being made over something that is sort of misty, and I think that you're trying to compromise my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, please refrain from comments. Please answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, Witness, if I can ask you to look at the top left, there is the reference number IK23/92. Can you just confirm that can you see that for me, please. That's all I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes, military court in Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution now have 65 ter number 31600. And I'm looking for page 77. My apologies, one page backwards to the start of his testimony on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going to read out some of your testimony to you, Mr. Milincic. We don't have this in B/C/S, unfortunately. This is during your examination-in-chief in the Krajisnik case. And the lawyer states: "Let's move on to a completely different topic, if we may. Tab 12, please. This relates, doesn't it, to the murder of Mr. Hadziselimovic, whom you told us had for a time being -- been the vice-president of the municipality. He had then, you've told us, resigned his seat within the assembly, and I think you told us he went to live elsewhere. Is that right?" And you answer: "Yes." The lawyer then states: "Now, let's not look at the first page, because I don't think that helps. The second page, which is the certificate with the Latin script, which is a document dated the 25th of March, 1996. Help us please. Top ..." And then it moves to the next page of the transcript. "... top left-hand corner it says 'vojni sud u Banja Luci.' Read that, please, top left-hand corner?" And then you answer: "Military court in Banja Luka, IK number 23/92, dated 25th of March, 1996." The lawyer then states: "We see then the name, Stanica. Continue reading it, please." And you answer: "Yes. Public security station Srbac. The following information is hereby ... delivered for the following convicted person, first and last names Ljubomir Stankovic, father's name Veljko, mother's name Koviljka, maiden name Sancanin, born on 30th of August, 1960, place of birth Saferovici village, Srbac municipality, socialist republic Srpska, resident at Saferovici village, Srbac municipality, Republika Srpska, ethnicity Serb, citizenship Republika Srpska, private by occupation worker. Date and number of judgement, 20th of March, 1995, IK number 23/92. The judgement handed down by the military court in Banja Luka for which offence, and it goes on to say, murder, under Article 26, paragraph 2, item 6, and the criminal offences of causing general danger under Article 172, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska. Sentence: Nine years of imprisonment. President of the Chamber, Captain First Class Svetozar Davidovic." And then you're asked: "How do we know which murder this refers to?" And you answer: "I asked to be sent -- I asked for it yesterday. I know who was murdered, but you don't, and of course I will not give a false statement. I know that it incurs responsibility. You can later on verify my testimony. An offence can be interpreted in different ways. The vice-president of the municipality ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we turn over the page, this quotation is almost finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The lawyer interrupts you and says: "Sorry, you're about to tell us. Just tell us who it is and how you know. Just tell us who it is that this individual murdered, and how you know who -- who it is?" And you answer: "Ljubomir Stankovic mentioned herein, shot the former councillor and vice-president of the assembly, Halid Hadziselimovic, who died several days later in the hospital as a result of his wounds." You then discuss briefly how you know this, and at line 13 of this page, you state: "This is the judgement handed down in relation to the same man, Stankovic, for that particular murder."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could go back to 65 ter 31607, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, perhaps I can ask you again: This is the document you brought and read out in the Krajisnik case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And in the Krajisnik case, you said this referred to the murder of Halid Hadziselimovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I stated that then, not knowing about some other things that had happened in the meantime. As for Halid, I was expressing interest because he was my vice-president. As for other incidents in the municipality, I -- I was not in charge. I could just receive information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I will turn to the crimes of Ljubomir Stankovic in a moment. When you were cross-examined in the Krajisnik case, you were shown the full judgement with this reference number and it was clear that it related to a completely different set of crimes. And you accepted that; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I really, really am being exposed here to the nitty-gritty of what I said and what I did not say. I mean, I'm not an expert. I am not involved in a court review or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, the question simply was whether it was put to you when you testified in the Krajisnik case that this judgement did not deal with this killing and that you accepted that. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's what I said then, then that's the way it is. I really cannot be a sorcerer now and remember what I said then. The president of the municipality did and said what he said. Now, I came here for Mladic, to say what is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now since you have no other documents that would compromise me, now you are trying to rehash this story three times and whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you want to us consider your testimony, you should answer the questions. You were called by the Mladic Defence. The parties this is this courtroom decide what questions will be put to you, and if the Judges have any additional questions they'll put those questions to you. You're supposed not to comment on relevance and importance because that's not for you to judge upon. And I do understand now that you say if that's what the transcript says in Krajisnik, you do not challenge that. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milincic, you say that we're trying to rehash this story three times, so let me just put the Prosecution position to you. You came in Krajisnik and you represented that this document showed Ljubomir Stankovic was convicted for the murder of Halid Hadziselimovic. That was shown to you to be incorrect; that that judgement referred to something else. And you've now come before this Trial Chamber in Mladic and you're making the same claim with that reference number, a claim you know to be incorrect. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is correct or incorrect. I know that this thing happened, that the man was tried. Now whether Halid was also ascribed to him, I don't know. Then I thought it was that way. Now I see it's different. Now I see that it's a fact that there were other things that he was tried for, but really I don't know. I showed it then, and that's why I brought it, to show the problems that we had during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I now turn to the substance of the crimes committed by Ljubomir Stankovic in Srbac. So he murdered Halid Hadziselimovic in May of 1992. After murdering Hadziselimovic, he is arrested but he's released shortly thereafter by the military authorities. That's right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's what I was told. When I reacted later, when I said, Why is this man free? And they said, We did not release him. It was the military court that did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And then in August of 1992, a few months later, he shoots four Muslims killing two and wounding two others. That's right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And he is released again, and we know this because in September 1994 he commits another crime, accidentally shooting and injuring two Serbian children?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Should I answer? Well, that's the way it was. But the president of the municipality was not a factor to arrest and try. My only mistake was that he was convicted for Halid and not the rest. I really don't see what more you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just asking you to confirm that's what happened in Srbac municipality with regard to Ljubomir Stankovic. What I've said is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's right. Those are facts that are not confirmed or challenged or attested to by the president of the municipality. I can talk to you about other crimes as well, those committed against Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but that's probably of no interest to you and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If you just care To answer my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please refrain from aggressively telling us what we should do, aggressively telling what Mr. MacDonald should do, and -- you're here to answer questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic was a member of the VRS, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Did I confirm that now? Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And as president and a member of the civilian authorities, you didn't have any authority over him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In fact, the best you could do was report him and ask that something be done about him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And you did report his crimes and ask that something be done, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: It wasn't I who reported it. Excuse me. I didn't reported it. I was only receiving information about what was happening. There are other services, police, the army, that were in charge of that, and they were just keeping the president abreast and highlighting what was important; that is to say, that not all the information reached my office but rather only such information that people believed to be important and that he would be of help in finding a solution. I don't know if you understand me. So it wasn't me who reported it when I heard about it, but I was informed about it only later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Were the crimes committed by Ljubomir Stankovic reported to the military authorities; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, because he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You had problems in Srbac with other soldiers coming on leave. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Are you aware if their crimes were also reported, just as Stankovic's were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of two or three cases, the killing of the Malesevic family. The perpetrators were detected later and prosecuted. There were attacks on Serbs and also on the Vejnovic family. We reported that as well. The Vejnovic family was beaten up and plundered. There were other instances of looting, harassment, et cetera. I was insisting more on some more relevant things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I seek to move to a new topic now but I'm aware of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to tender any of the -- I take it not -- the transcript? And is this one in evidence, the 2392 IK --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: There is a judgement relating to it, Your Honour, but I would tender 65 ter 31607, which is the document the witness brought which also refers to that judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31607 receives number P6918, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the judgement is already in evidence as P03538, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- yes. We take a break, Mr. Milincic. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you've spoken about your efforts to maintain in Davor but, in fact, as early as 1993, you advocated the taking of international personnel as hostages, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought the question had talked about at first to maintain peace, it's misstating the evidence if it's indicating that there's a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can, I'll simply ask the question, Mr. Milincic. In 1993, you advocated the taking of international personnel as hostages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I have to explain a wider context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to be described as being aggressive again, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one used -- oh, you mean that I used "aggressively." That was when you instructed the parties that they should do in this courtroom. That's something totally different from answering a question. The question simply was whether you, in 1993, whether you advocated the taking of international personnel as hostages for and whatever reasons, if Mr. MacDonald would like to know. But the reasons he'll ask you about it. But did you advocate that in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But on condition that I'm allowed to explain in what context I said that. Yes, yes, I did say that, but I would like to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in re-examination, Mr. Ivetic will have an opportunity to further explore the backgrounds of why you did that and whether you may have done it for good reasons, I do not know. But at this moment have you to answer Mr. MacDonald's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 02366.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going to show you your words, Mr. MacDonald. This is the transcript from the 24th session of Republika Srpska Assembly on 8th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm looking for page 80 in the English and I believe page 55 in the B/C/S. Or perhaps page 79 in the English to see the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, you recall being at this session and speaking at this special?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milincic, if I can direct you to the last part of your speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, it was the last paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You state: "We also have something to blackmail them with. Homeini and his team held a very small number of Americans in the American embassy in Tehran and shook America quite well. Well, we also have enough of those white men or the others and that can be used as our weapon." You're advocating hostage-taking as a weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's difficult to -- mm-hm is -- on the transcript doesn't show as a "yes" or a "no." And I do understand that you agree that you are advocating hostage-taking as a weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of your statement, you say there were 879 non-Serbs in Srbac and that only 60 of them moved away, mainly for economical reasons. But, in fact, many more non-Serbians -- non-Serbian citizens left during the war, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I didn't have exact records. And as for those who appealed to me and asked to be allowed to cross over to Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his answer. It was too quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat the end of your answer there, Mr. Milincic. You spoke too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: We're talking about numbers here. The number is 800 -- no, 60. Sixty-something people left for third countries, whereas you say that there were more of them. I'm telling you again that not all of them reported to me. Whenever I intervened for people to be able to cross over, that would be approximately the number as stated here. Am I being clear enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, may I draw your attention to the following. If this is what you intended to say in your statement, then you should have said a small number of them, around 60 persons, reported to me because they wished to leave the municipality. Because there is a difference and you -- I think you would be aware of that, that saying that 60 people moved out is not the same as I know of 60 people who reported to me that they wished to move out, because there may have been others who did not report to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the statement in this respect is not accurate. But we now better understand what you intended to say. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Do you accept that, in fact, the majority of the Muslim and Croat population in Srbac in 1991 had left by 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, I cannot accept that. I cannot be precise, but I wouldn't say a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P03853.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, this is an overview of data on the number and ethnic structure of the population according to the municipalities by the Banja Luka Department of State Security, and it refers to 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can have page 6 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, sir, here we see Srbac, 1991, Muslims 940; Croats, 145. In 1995, we see Muslims, 300; Croats, 50. Now this document, sir, shows that over two-thirds of the Muslims had departed and almost two-thirds of the Croats had departed. Do you now accept that the majority of Croats and Muslims left Srbac --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that. I can see these facts. I didn't had them before, I mean this information, and as a person who was in the civilian authorities, I was never presented with this kind of report. Yes, it's all right. This is a fact. I didn't believe that the majority left, but it seems that they had. All I wanted to add was that quite a few Serbs also left for other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you're explaining this to say, I never received this information but you believed. This Chamber is not interested primarily in what you believe but is primarily interested in what you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, therefore, you perhaps should have refrained from giving firm statements on the matter if you don't know. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald. By the way, I have another question. In your statement you say in 1991 that 95 per cent of the population was Serb, whereas this data makes 90 per cent of the population Serb. Less than 90.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question? Well, you know, we politicians, we usually say around 90 per cent. Unfortunately that's how we communicate. There is no statistical accuracy. Even nowadays if somebody asks me how many of them there are, I would say between 80 and 90 per cent. So there's no accuracy there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't give a statement as a politician but you did give a statement as a witness and you said 95 per cent, whereas at least in this data for 1991 it gives a little bit less than 90 per cent of Serbs. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is important, that is what I thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My problem is that in your statement apparently no clear distinction is made between what you think, what you believe, and, on the one hand side, and on the other hand, what you know, and that is what we are interested in. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, before I move away from this topic, I'm not suggesting you've seen this document before. What I'm suggesting that your position that in Srbac people only left for economical reasons and there was no large leaving is entirely incorrect, and as president of Srbac you would have known that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: You are chastising me. I know that people were leaving. But as for this data, I didn't know about that. Not that I wasn't expected to know, but I was facing more serious problems. How many people left every day, it is difficult to keep a tab on that and to keep any records. The whole area was being emptied. Everybody was running away, including the Serbs. People were leaving. And now if you look at it through a magnifying-glass, then we have what we have. And you interpret it in your way, which is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- Witness, again, would you please refrain from making these kind of sweeping general statements which do not assist in any way the Chamber, neither does it assist the party that calls you or the party that is opposed to that party. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we please have the witness's statement on the screen. It is D783. It is paragraph 4 which interests me which is on page 3 in the English, and I believe -- it begins on page 2 in the B/C/S, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read out the translation of your statement on this matter and you can tell me if it's correct, what it says in the B/C/S versions of your statement. Starting at the top of page 3 in the English: "A total of 879 non-Serbs faced the 1990s on their hearths. A small number of them, around 60 persons, moved out during the war, mainly for economic reasons. The situation is almost the same today ..." That's what you said in your statement, isn't it, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you re-start your answer. The interpreters were unable to catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This figure, 60, should mean 60 families. That would be more appropriate than what is says here, 60 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Does it say 60 persons in the B/C/S version of your statement, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that it says "lica," that means "persons." Now I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And your position, the position you've maintained up until today -- Mr. Milincic, if you wait a second. Sorry. If you wait for my question, please. The position you've maintained up until today is that 60 persons moved out for economic reasons but the situation is the same. That's just not true in 1995, in any case, is it, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Most of the families returned. I don't know how many because I wasn't the president of the municipality after 1997. Therefore, I don't know. And the term today or nowadays is a relative one. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So you're now accepting that these relatively large numbers of Muslims and Croats had left the municipality and had not returned by 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Until 1995, yes, it could be true. But as for nowadays, I don't know. Because the war wasn't over by 1995. I don't know if you're referring to 1995 or 2005?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm referring to what the document shows, the one I just showed you, which is, by 1995, over two-thirds of the Muslims and almost two-thirds of the Croats had left Srbac, the municipality you were a president of. I'll just finally to ask you to agree that that's correct and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that on the whole this is accurate. I know that Serbs were moving out as well, but that is not important at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can move on. Mr. Milincic, a mosque in Kobas burned down on 11th of July, 1993. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Kobas is in Srbac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And the perpetrators or those who burned it down were not identified, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Not during my term of office, and I don't think that they have ever been identified. So you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll now turn to a new topic. You were an SDS --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: May I just add something to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If you can just answer my questions, Mr. Milincic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: And it's relating to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's direct in relation to the question that was put to you, you may. If it's not, you may not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last time I also stated that there was a commission formed by the police and the court that fire department went to extinguish the fire, and the next day the police determined the cause of the fire, but to this date it wasn't clear what happened. There were three versions, whether it was done by the Serbs, whether it was caused by lightening, or it was possibly burned by the Muslims themselves fearing retaliation and they wanted this to be a kind of provocation. This has not been resolved to this very day. I would like to know what the outcome is and I would like to have it to insert it in the book that I'm currently writing, and I mean who set the mosque on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, this last part is not related to the question. The first part of what you added did relate to the question. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You were a member of the Main Board of the SDS from 1990 until 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 17134. This is a list of SDS Main Board members in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'll be looking for page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of this document, we see your name and contact details; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And this document, in fact, provides a work and home telephone number as well as an address for SDS Main Board members, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Do you recall if you had a document like this during your time as a Main Board member?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember. It is possible, but I don't have it in my files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution would move to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under relevance, what the probative value of -- the witness says that he was a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, but he's confirmed that the other people there were also members of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- if you consider that -- "and this document, in fact, provides work and home telephone number as well as address for SDS Main Board member, doesn't it?" If you consider a confirmation of that, then you should have been more explicit. Could you have a look at the names on this list. It was suggested to you that these were all members of the Main Board of the SDS. Do you find any name in there which you know not to be a member of the Main Board of the SDS. Apart from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I think that this is probably authentic. Most probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, authentic or not, but you -- it's your recollection there's -- the persons on this list were members of the SDS Main Board.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It still leaves open time-frame, Mr. MacDonald. But at least these persons, as the witness says, were at a point in time, members of the SDS Main Board. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, first, I should decide on admission. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17134 receives number P6919, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Srbac set up a Crisis Staff in 1992; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's probably right. I cannot confirm it. If there's some written record of that, and I'm sure there is, and last time I did bring minutes of the meetings of the Crisis Staff, but I cannot give you an exact date. We had Crisis Staffs and a War Presidency. Crisis Staffs were a continuation of the former Yugoslavia. They had been set up in case of floods and earthquakes and other disasters, and then they acted accordingly during war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31609. This is an excerpt from the Srbac Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It is Article 1 that I'm interested in, Mr. Milincic. Can you read it and then confirm that this is the decision setting up the Crisis Staff in Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We see it's dated 28th May. If I can ask that the B/C/S be scrolled up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the translation doesn't say that it was made in 28th of May, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We only had the first article translated, Your Honour, but I'm happy to confirm with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, does this refresh your memory, was a Crisis Staff in Srbac set up on 28th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The date is stated up here, and I cannot deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It was set up pursuant to an order from the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I do not see here on the basis of what, just the Statute of the municipality of Srbac. I cannot see. I mean, you are referring to a decision of the ARK Krajina, but I do not see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness -

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I do not see the letterhead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question is whether it was pursuant to an order of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina, not whether the document says so but whether you have a recollection that it was set up pursuant to an order of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Was it or was it not or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll accept that. I'll accept that. With a risk, yes. I mean, really, let us not have a polemic here, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you say you accept that, it means that you don't know. Because you add that there's a risk involved. If you don't know, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would rather decide on a yes. Because the document is not written here but memory is memory so I would accept yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you at the first question respond with a yes? The question was put to you. Your final answer now is yes. Not because the document says but because you remember. Why not immediately say: I remember that it was. It saves a lot of time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right. I mean, I'm a serious man, a responsible man. I want to assist us all. So, yes, as for this automatic thing why I didn't say so immediately, you know what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Just listen to the question, answer them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let it be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Did you become president of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I signed it, so yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31600.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milincic, I'm just looking to refresh your memory regarding the Autonomous Region of Krajina order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It's page 41 that I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is your Krajisnik testimony, sir. If we look from line 9 onwards, the lawyer in that case asked you: "Was a Crisis Staff formed?" You answered: "Yes." He asked you why, and your answer was: "At some point in 1992, we received an order from AR Krajina, and AR Krajina, once again, was an institution referring to the Krajina municipalities gravitating around Banja Luka." Just to confirm, sir, I appreciate we've discussed this already, but just to confirm, you accept the Crisis Staff in Srbac was set up following an order from the Autonomous Region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can now move to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can now move to the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina. When that was formed, the presidents of the municipalities like yourself became members. That's right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And you attended meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And you heard about violence, including killings, against Croats and Muslims in other municipalities of the ARK, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Where? Crisis Staff of the ARK Krajina? No, no. Comments could have been sort of in the couloirs but nothing official. I didn't receive any or provide any. I mean, nothing official. The motive of our meetings was something else and why the ARK Krajina and why I went from Srbac to the ARK Krajina. I was interested in wood, crude oil, survival. Not crimes. I mean, somebody from Srbac to talk about that. I mean, give me a concrete question and I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Either officially or unofficially, you heard about crimes against Muslims and Croats, including killings, in the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, what I heard about more was crimes against Serbs at the time. Of course, this was heard as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, whether you heard more about other things, if you're asked about it, please tell us. But the question was whether you heard about killings of Muslims and Croats in the ARK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At official meetings I did not hear that. Unofficially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was already part of the question. Officially or unofficially. Do I understand that when I interrupted you, that you were about to say that you did hear of that unofficially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to move to some statements made by certain people now. Vojislav Kupresanin was the president of the ARK Assembly. And you know him, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Know him to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we have 65 ter number 02366, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is a transcript from the 24th Session of the RS Assembly on 8th January, 1993. It is the one we looked at earlier when you spoke about hostage taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: At this time if we have page 77 of the English and 52 of the B/C/S, please. Perhaps if we can go back one page in the English - my apologies - to see who is speaking. Or back two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is Mr. Kupresanin speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can ask the English be brought forward two pages now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm looking at part of his speech where he says, or he begins: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I cannot find it. Probably it is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It may be on --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I believe that you are interpreting it the way it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It may be on the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It must be a different page. It's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can I ask to look now, sir, I think it may be near the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you guiding the witness to the top of the B/C/S page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Not of this page, Your Honours. I think it's -- well, perhaps if I can check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, the bottom paragraph, the name of the speaker --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I just cannot find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I don't think it's on this page. It's clear that at the top Mr. Kupresanin -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot find it. Yes, yes, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which -- it's you who should find it, Mr. MacDonald, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I thought I had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, can I just check the name of the speaker, the last speaker on this page in the B/C/S, that is Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I believe it's the start of the first or the second paragraphs. The sentence stating: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, it's the third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm obliged to my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then could you also have a look at 3 to 5 or 3 to -- 5 to 6. The easiest way to find your way often is by looking at numbers. I see -- in the paragraph in English I see 3 to 5 clearly appearing. In the B/C/S, however, I see at approximately the same place 5 to 6 which may illustrate an error. I'm not saying it is, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going read out that text to you, Mr. Milincic, where Kupresanin states: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary. Right now, if we were to count the population right now, there would be...," and the next word is either "over" or "about" "... a million Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina would be predominantly a Serb republic. Is war necessary in Serbia? It's a horrible thing to say that war would be necessary in Serbia. If Serbia does not go into the war now, then in three to five years the Albanians and Muslims will be entirely legally overtaking the power in Belgrade, along with the Serb opposition. This war was necessary for the Serb people." Now, Mr. Milincic, this quotation was read to you in Krajisnik, and you were asked the following question? "Q. Mr. Milincic, isn't Mr. Kupresanin and that body before all those delegates acknowledging the reduction of the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a reduction that took place through massive forcible expulsions. Isn't that what that's a reference to?" And your answer was: [As read] "Yes, those are the facts." When you said that, you were telling the truth to the Krajisnik Trial Chamber that those were the facts, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Are you speaking about Mr. Kupresanin's remarks during the discussion? Is that what you're referring to, whether that is a fact or not? So you asked me whether he said that, and you say that in the Krajisnik case I confirmed that that was the case. Do we have a correlation here? So the question is what? Whether Kupresanin did say that or not? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I have read out to you what Kupresanin said. I have read out to you that --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: -- in answer to the question posed to you in the Krajisnik you said, "Yes, those are the facts," and I'm asking you whether you told the truth to the Krajisnik Trial Chamber, that those were the facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Krajisnik Trial Chamber had two questions posed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the transcript on the screen, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Can the Prosecution have 65 ter number 31600. And it is page 126. And the quotation that was read out is the page before, Your Honours. I'm happy to go back to it if Your Honours wish. The question is at the top from line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if you slowly read the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, in Krajisnik, you were asked: "Mr. Milincic, isn't Mr. Kupresanin in that body, before all those delegates, acknowledging the reduction of the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a reduction that took place through massive forcible expulsions? Isn't that what that's a reference to?" And you answered: "Yes. Those are ... facts." What you said in Krajisnik, your comment upon Kupresanin's statement, is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I said that that is what the member of parliament said in the discussion. I am not saying that that is a fact in terms of that being the factual situation. He presented his view of the situation, which the assembly did not adopt. So this is just free discussion. It's a fact that he took part in the debate, like many other people do. Very forcefully, very emotionally. Sometimes perhaps in a way that is not exactly moderate. But in the debate people can say whatever they wish. However, the conclusions cannot be just anything. So when I say it is a fact, it is a fact that Medic and Kupresanin did take part in the discussion very forcefully, very emotionally, but this was not adopted by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's your interpretation of those words. By the way, you did not say that that is a fact but you said those are facts. Let's move on, Mr. MacDonald. And could you please have the translation verified. Because if you look at the beginning of the paragraph of the document you've shown us before, then it seems that these are all separate sentences, whereas at least in the one language it's different from the other one. Apart from the 3 to 5 which suddenly becomes 5 to 6. So therefore, there's a real need to carefully review that translation also in view of the first two sentences where the first sentence apparently says something which is immediately then contradicted by the second: Was it necessary? It was necessary or it was not necessary. That's -- raises quite a few questions. Please have it verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll have it verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, did you know an Aleksa Milijevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Milojevic, is that who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Milojevic, yes. He is an economist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
