utterances.text: And was he the Republika Srpska minister for spatial planning and development?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not the one then. Then maybe this surname is correct what is written here, Milijevic. I do know an Aleksa Milojevic, though. I said yes a moment ago with Aleksa Milojevic in mind, but this other person, Milijevic, as I see here, even if he was there at the time I don't seem to remember him, the one you said was minister for spatial planning and development.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps can I move past this topic. Witness, in -- moving to a new topic, in paragraph 17 of your statement, you discuss the transfer the 22.000 people from Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia. The 22.000 people you discuss, they were Muslims and Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one more topic with the witness, but perhaps given the time, I don't think I'll finish in the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm looking at you, Mr. Ivetic, and I'm also looking at Mr. Mladic. If it's a matter of a couple of minutes, would you prefer to have the break now and have the cross-examination concluded after the break or would you rather want to know the whole content of the cross-examination before we take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would defer to my client. Mr. Stojanovic is asking him. My client is asking for the break to be taken now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we will take the break. But we have taken note, Mr. MacDonald, of the time estimate you gave. The witness will be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: A couple of quick housekeeping matters, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I think Your Honour may have misheard when I -- just before the break I said I will not be finished in the next couple of minutes rather than I will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I hope to be finished in under ten minutes, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is a that wishful thinking. Perhaps that's ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The first of the last two matters, if I -- I forgot to tender a document, that's 31609. That was the excerpt from the Srbac Official Gazette. The witness confirmed at temporary transcript page 38 the date and the establishment, so I seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, but that was the one where the header was not translated into English. I don't know if Your Honours still had a concern about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, if the parties agree that it is the 28th of May, 1992, then I would say that there's no urgent need to send it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I can stipulate on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness testified about it. Madam Registrar, 65 ter 31609 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P6920, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6920 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness clarified that the date is correct, which could have been seen on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And finally, the Prosecution would like to marked for identification 65 ter 02366. That is the transcript we were discussing just before the break, the Kupresanin speech, and just the relevant pages, Your Honours. I would put them as pages 75 to 77 in the English and 52 to 53 in the B/C/S. I am aware Your Honour raised the question about verification here and that's why I would seek to mark it for identification pending discussion with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, you know as always, if the Defence feels the need that for contextualisation you would need other pages, that you always can bring this to the attention of the Prosecution and the Chamber so that we don't have to go in two rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the Prosecution should upload page one so that we know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And has it been uploaded separately, the pages you selected, because if not we can reserve a number but we cannot yet MFI it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm informed by colleagues it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm informed it hasn't been uploaded separately and that's my fault. My apologies, Your Honours. But we would appreciate a number being reserved at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then you have to already indicate under what new number you would then upload it into e-court. A small A perhaps might do. That would therefore be 02366a for which, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reserved number would be P6921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That number is reserved. Apart from the pages you indicated also the cover page in both languages has to be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm obliged Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, in paragraph 9 of your statement, you mention a statement by Karadzic comparing nations with flowers and saying that they are best when interwoven. Now that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In actual fact, Mr. Karadzic [Realtime transcript read in error "Krnjajic"] repeatedly offered analogies showing that nations could not live together, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: This is a paradox, isn't it? He is saying that the garden is the most beautiful when there is a variety of flowers. How can this question come up now? We have just confirmed that he want this is variegated pattern, so how all of a sudden can they not live together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 13386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And before we do that, Mr. MacDonald, just check at page 51, line 15, whether it's Mr. Krnjajic or Karadzic you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It is Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is at page 12 in the English and page 18 in the B/C/S, and I should say this is a record of the 14th Session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska on the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I believe the second paragraph in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And it's also the second paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And it states: "National communities --" my apologies. It states: "I don't want to say that this is something specific to the Balkans. National communities which cannot live together do exist in the middle of Europe. They cannot because they hinder each other's development? "In the plant world there are plants which cannot grow side by side. They have to be separated to flourish." Can you confirm you see that text for me?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I was talking about a rally on the 2nd of September, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please answer the question. The simple question was is whether the words read by Mr. MacDonald, whether you see them, and then wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we please go back a page in the English and the B/C/S. My apologies. Two pages in each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you're under estimating sometimes the length of the speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Indeed. I believe it's one more page in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And we see this is Dr. Radovan Karadzic who's giving this speech. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Milincic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I can see this text here. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. MacDonald, for purely practical purposes, I'm also looking at Mr. Ivetic, we always go back. Now, that's fine. But if it undisputed who is speaking, then you just put it to the witness. And if Mr. Ivetic would disagree, then I'm sure that he will jump up and bring this to our attention. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, this is Karadzic using another plant analogy but this time to show that peoples cannot live together, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is written here. As for your previous question, that relates to the meet -- the rally in Srbac in 1990, the garden, the flowers, et cetera. So this is a different thing. I was quoting the words from the rally in Srbac. I'm not aware of this because I was not a member of the parliament and I don't know if this is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, the Prosecution would seek to tender the relevant pages. I apologise, again it's not been uploaded separately, that is my fault, but we would like to reserve a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And then you would have to indicate what number -- I take it that we add a small A to the number. Let me have a look. It's 13386a, which will receive.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Reserve number P6922, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved. And please, again, cover page and selection of pages. And, Mr. Ivetic, if there is need for contextualisation we'll hear you from. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Finally, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I would like 65 ter number 22399a. And this is a short video-clip, Your Honours. And there are both B/C/S and English transcripts that have been given to the booths. The clip is approximately one minute and 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we have to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll play it twice, Mr. Milincic, so therefore it is -- it's for technical reasons. So you have two opportunities to listen to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "[VOICEOVER]: Mr. President, dear members of the Presidency, assemblymen, ladies and gentlemen, dear guests. This is the 21st Session of our assembly and the path that is behind us is so rich that many things occur between two sessions. This is actually the path that gradually brought us to our state, taking us from an artificial state in which we were forcibly held in an artificial creation that is Bosnia and Herzegovina together with our centuries-old foes. It all reminds me of the experiment in which a dog and a cat are held in a box together against their will, or a bad marriage maintained by all sorts of forceful means. It transpired that a dog and a cat can remain in the box together under one condition only, namely, that they lose their natural characteristics and cease to be a dog and a cat. We will remember that we could not be Serbs and live in such a box. I assume that neither the Croats nor the Muslims had an easy time and that they also had to give up their natural identity and culture, but they gave up less, and I don't hold it against them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, this is Karadzic using a dog and cat analogy to show his belief that the ethnicities could not live together, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: This poetic language and this metaphor, are you expecting me to say yes or no? He just took a poetic licence and he said what he said. I constantly keep comparing the rally in 1990 and the vision of the future Bosnia-Herzegovina in which we would have been able to live together. That was a few years before. I talked about colourful flowers and the need for the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats to live together, and I [as interpreted] said whoever wants war should ask the Serbian, Muslim, and Croat mothers whether they wanted war, and I received an applause for that. Now you're asking me weather he said this or are you asking me if I agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Milincic, firstly I should say you have been recorded on the transcript as saying you talked about colourful flowers and about asking Serbian, Muslim, and Croat mothers, but I believe you meant Karadzic spoke -- Karadzic said those word, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now to go back to my question. You bring up in your statement this phrase by Karadzic about a garden being beautiful when it's interwoven with different colours and flowers, and what I'm suggesting to that you is Karadzic said the opposite and what I've shown you and that peoples could not live together. And you accept that's what he said on these other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: What I heard on the tape, I can confirm that I heard what I heard. It's not up to me to evaluate how his thoughts developed between 1990 and 1994 when he said this. So I confirm that I understand what he said in this audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, the question whether the witness accepts is that what he said, is the question is this a fraudulent tape or is it a real tape of what the witness said -- of what Mr. Karadzic said? Now, the witness has not been present, at least it has not been established, so it's a rather useless question. This is what Mr. Karadzic apparently said. We see it on the video. Now what apparently you're interested to know is whether the witness having looking at this video, Mr. Milincic, whether you would agree with Mr. MacDonald, that Karadzic used language, perhaps at another moment, which is still in biological terms but is not emphasizing how nice it is to live together, and whether have you any -- first of all, whether you agree with him that that other language was used by Mr. Karadzic and then I take it that the next question would be whether he has any comment on these rather different expressions of thoughts by Mr. Karadzic. So let's first focus on the first question: Do you agree that Mr. Karadzic used language which goes in an entirely different direction at another point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in that case. But speaking about Srbac, it was always insisted that there should be peace because he said that as far as Srbac goes, there's place for everyone. Now when we speak about Srbac, he always tried, speaking about the Muslims, to have them in Srbac and Kobas and everything else. So it's a different context. He never asked me to do what he is talking about here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer and slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slowly repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever I met President Karadzic, he was always interested to hear about the situation in Srbac, what was going on with the Muslims in Crnaja, it's a village, and Kobas. He warned me if you are afraid, then -- to have 1.000 Serbs as opposed to 21.000, then you're not good men and not good people because you in Srbac must preserve all the people you have there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I therefore understand your explanation is that when he used the flower example, that that was in relation to Srbac, and the cat and the dog --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- he may have used it for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not a deputy of the assembly. I never heard this speech and believe me, or not, this is the first time that I'm hearing it. If you are seeking my opinion, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I asked you to comment on the two different -- two rather different expressions of mind by Mr. Karadzic. So if you, in that context, if you could give me your comment, then please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that he had a good reason to react as he did here, just as he had reasons to encourage us that we be a garden with all colourful flowers, and the Serbs Croats and the Muslims. That is why he said ask the Serbian, the Muslim, and the Croat mothers if they wanted war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now can you reconcile the statement about the cats and the dogs, impossible to live in one cage without losing their identity, can you reconcile that with the flowers in Srbac? Because Muslims and Serbs or Croats are, in Srbac, still different groups, not in -- as far as I can understand at this moment, but please help me, not any different from Serbs and Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srbac has some specific features. They were both ideological and ethnic conflicts, and this was shown in the last election as well. But let me go back to your question. Probably the chronology of the events, the breakup of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this severe settling of accounts prompted him to say something and to make a comparison with a cat and dog. Probably at the time he had good arguments to speak as he did, and unfortunately he was telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, truth or not. But your comment is that talking about the cats and dogs, that was at a later point in time and that may explain the difference, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I simply seek to tender the video-clip, Your Honours. I will ask for it to be MFI'd just now. We don't have a physical CD with the clip on it, and my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the transcript in both languages has been uploaded. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22399a receives number P6923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If this works? Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And so is the microphone, I understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day again, sir. I would like to start off by discussing Mr. Ljubomir Stankovic who was discussed in cross-examination. In regards to Mr. Stankovic, can you tell us if you at all took part in the trial that took place against him and which rendered a judgement against him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I don't know that man. I don't know him at all. I may have met him somewhere, but I don't know him. I never had any meeting with him and I never participated in any resolutions. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the Prosecution counsel referred to additional documentation that the Prosecution received about this individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P3538 is the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it describes that Mr. Stankovic was actually convicted for the murder of two Muslims, the wounding of two other Muslims, and the wounding of two Serbs. I'd like to take a look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: D783, and page 4 in both versions of the same, and it will be in paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the last bullet point in paragraph 13 talks about the murder and wounding of two Muslims, Bosniaks at Kobas, committed by the same perpetrator who committed the previous came, and it was subsequently discovered that he had in the meantime also wounded two Serb children. Are these the same persons, do you believe, as in the judgement that has been referred to by the Prosecution against Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a dispute about this matter, Mr. Ivetic? Because we heard the witness say earlier that he's not a lawyer, he doesn't know anything, he's -- and that you even had some problems with IK23/92 being put to him claiming that it should be put to him. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is there any dispute about the matter? Because to hear the explanation of the witness who says that he is not very able to interpret legal documents, if you all agree that it's about two Muslims killed at Kobas by Halid Hadziselimovic and the wounding of two -- and two children being wounded, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would be happy to agree if we all can agree that this statement is the same as the -- the recollection in the statement is the same as the recollection in the judgement, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was whether what is stated here in rather abstract terms, whether that reflects what is found in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you agree on that, then we don't have to ask further questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think I have to correct my Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's always possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not two Muslims killed by that person, Halid Hadziselimovic, but by Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry, yes. I'm mixing up the victim with the -- with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Accused. I think we all understand each other so that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should be very careful to do that, that -- not so cautious not to do -- to make such a mistake. Is there agreement between the parties that is what is described in the last bullet point, that that is what is found in the judgement of which we just received a number, and I think it was P3538, if my recollection serves me will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The last bullet point refers to that judgement, not the third bullet point in the statement as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm focusing on the last one and there is agreement on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'd like to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1993 and the speech that you gave in relation to the taking of international personnel as hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to that again and that's now 02366, page 55 in the B/C/S and 75 in the English. I apologise, I think it's page 65 in the B/C/S. 66 in the B/C/S -- or pardon me. Now I'm all over the place. It should be, I think, the -- it should be ten pages prior in the B/C/S on -- the ERN number 925 at the end. Those are your words. And then that should be at -- I have here listed, page 75 in the English. Is that 75? Then it's not that one. Then it's going to be page 81 in the English perhaps. The prior page in English. Yes. The prior page in English. It should be in the beginning of the -- this is the tail-end of the discussion where Mr. MacDonald focused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have the right pages now before us, isn't it, about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The speech actually starts on the prior page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English, yes. But there's no disagreement about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said the words --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, first of all, your statements made to the assembly in 1993, were they adopted as an official position of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: In response to my desperate thinking, similar to the Kupresanin's speech, it wasn't included in the conclusions. However, seeing that there's a war raging around us, that we were being killed, that there were cease-fires and then again everybody was charging against everyone, and I made analogy about a lamb and a wolf, and I said that lamb was innocent. I also mentioned Homeini, who held American hostages in the American embassy, and I said what are we a waiting for? Let us try and bring some of their people to make them understand us and take us seriously and to show them what they are doing to us. This was a kind of desperate opinion that I presented to the assembly. Later on, the general tried to calm down these feisty discussions. So this fully corresponds to what I said if you put it in the context of the time in which we were guilty a priori, and I can tell you that that "a priori" means "in advance," because I studied that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You made reference to the general trying to calm things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In fact, the general speaks two pages later in the B/C/S, and it is page, I think, 83, in the English. If we can turn there right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I would ask for you to read slowly General Mladic's entire selection which starts on this page and concludes at the top of the next page in the B/C/S, but first read what's on this page, so we can hear what General Mladic said during this rather heated debate.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Since this was a crucial session, presidents of municipalities were invited to attend. I happened to be there and I provided my angle of viewing things, and Mr. Mladic took to the floor and said the following: "I apologise to the deputies, but 30 minutes ago 35 airplanes took of the Kennedy plane carrier and are flying in an unidentified direction. They are not reflected in our radar systems, but they probably head towards Iran. Or, rather, Iraq. Iraq refused to withdraw its rockets to the south of the 35th parallel, and this ultimatum by America, France, and England expired one hour ago. I would not like to influence any decision of the deputies, but I urge you not to appear too heated and too threatening. Let us not create more damage to ourselves than necessary. "Next, if you please, I shall use this opportunity to relate some sad news to you. We are dealing in politics too much at all levels. We become sleepy, we become deadened on the front line, and then unfortunately we had surprises, this one in Kravica which can be connected to our traditional celebrations but also to other problems. We had an unfortunate event today near the Rilici village at Kupres due to the lack of attention of those who were guarding the front line - people, officers, commanders, group commanders - a group of Ustashas made an ambush to a vehicle transporting food on which many civilians are also loaded. They shot from the ambush from Zolja and there were ten casualties among the civilians and soldiers, and eight were wounded. Each Serbian life is more important than any canton, figuratively speaking, or any province. I urge you to protect the people and we shall do this which working and not by talking. "I don't know how we are going to appear at the conference in Geneva because of the situation such as the following. At around 1500 hours today an airplane arrived to Sarajevo airport from Turkey, probably with some delegation from Turkey and some Mujahedins, who were most likely going to Kiseljak. Hakijab Turajlic [phoen], vice-president of this faulty government of BH, was in an UNPROFOR car together with Colonel Sartre, a French. Our people stopped and searched the vehicle and one of our soldiers killed this man called Turajlic with six bullets."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then on this -- on this page it also says "aplauz."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to the next page in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could finish with what General Mladic said to calm the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it was the next page in B/C/S. On top there is -- there is -- that's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could read the rest of General Mladic's presentation.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Please, please, I ask you not to develop such a climate towards UNPROFOR. There are those who work well too. We shall protest sharply. I ordered that a protest be written and sent to Nambiar. And I told them the last time that the UN and UNPROFOR are not the service or the logistics of Alija Izetbegovic or Franjo Tudjman or ours, but we still have to pay attention, we must have a very, very sober head. I ask you not to let some individual drive us to disaster. That's all and thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, first of all, do you remember what kind of effect General Mladic's words had on the attendees of this assembly, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, then, and also now, given the time distance, I understood in this pyramid that after all that has to be respected. What the person who knows more and who took care of more. I took care of just one particular setting, and the general had all of us in his soul. He had to take care of us and he was calming people down so that our misfortune would not become even greater. Srbac is also grateful for what we lived to see - namely, that we did not go to war - and I am conveying the views of the people of Srbac, conveying their gratitude to the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are not here to present the thoughts of your people. You are here to testify about your personal knowledge about certain events. That's what you are here for. And apparently you have difficulties in understanding that. But wait for the next question that Mr. Ivetic will put to you and then answer that. Are you still with the same subject matter, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in his speech General Mladic references Kravica. Do you know what had happened on Serb Christmas of January 1993 prior to this assembly that General Mladic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I'd object to that. I'm not sure how that arises from cross-examination, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, an opportunity is always given to give the context of a portion of -- presented by you as a meeting, and if for the understanding of the context further questions are put to the witness, then Mr. Ivetic is allowed to do so. Could you briefly explain what happened in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, many people think and future analysts will probably say that they were a cause --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or consequence of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, a crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I stop you there. You are not invited to comment on how other people will explain certain situations. You're invited to tell us what you know about what happened in Kravica as referred to during that meeting by General Mladic. Could you please tell us what happened in Kravica, to the extent you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that Muslims committed a crime in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further details? How many victims, were of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No. No, many victims. Now how many is many? Well, different figures were bandied about. Hundred, thousands. This is an area far away from Srbac. I heard that the Muslims had committed a massacre there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the victims were of what ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb victims, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was what had happened in Kravica known to yourself and other assembly-persons at the time that the words were uttered at this assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I heard it at the time. I assume that those who were closer to there knew more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to a different topic. I would like to talk with you about the mosque in Kobas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask some --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- additional questions in relation to this. Witness, I -- I do understand that Mr. Ivetic asked you questions about what Mr. Mladic said, so as -- that he would have calmed down, where you had suggested that taking of hostages might be a weapon. I'm, in that respect, a bit confused because from what you read from this transcript, the very last portion says, I ask you not to develop such climate towards the UNPROFOR, et cetera, that's certainly calming done. And the paragraph before that, Mr. Mladic refers to Mr. Turajlic being, if I read it well, just being executed, which is met with applause. So I'm a bit confused as to what is the calming down portion and where it is not calming down at all but it seems to be happy about a violent event. Could you tell us how we have to understand this in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a logical question, a logical line of thought. The general said that an incident had occurred, a stupid thing, and a man was killed. And the deputies did what they did. It's not that the general instigated them. He said we are creating incidents, here is this most recent case, he submitted this information, and applause followed. Masses, a gathering of people, who are hurt. They seek an adequate measure. That is the psychology of the masses at a moment like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now better understand that when he referred to the incident where Mr. Turaljic was killed, that he used that as a trigger to calm everyone down and say this is not what should happen. Now I better understand the context. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let me just for sake of -- of clarity, since I think the Kupresanin speech is also in this assembly before General Mladic's speech, was the speech of Mr. Kupresanin adopted as official policy by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It was not adopted in the conclusions or it wasn't in the record. He is a patriot who likes strong language, but he is a person who helped many Muslims as well. But again he gets carried away with a historic mission and then he says what he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. Mr. MacDonald, did you ask these questions suggesting that this was formally adopted or was that you wanted to highlight the attitude of the speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It was just the attitude of the speakers, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to talk about the mosque in Kobas that Mr. MacDonald asked you about. First, can you tell us how the fire in the mosque was reported and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: In Kobas we had a police check-point, and during the night the police informed the firemen in Srbac, telling them that the mosque was on fire. I brought the duty book last time. The firemen raced there but that is 20 kilometres away from Srbac. Unfortunately, it was too late. The mosque was mainly made of wood. On the following day, a municipal commission went out to investigate with the police and an investigating judge and they compiled a record. To this day it is unknown how it was that the mosque was set on fire. There are three versions. I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think you already mentioned the three versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've told us already. Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from what I understand there was a clear suggestion in the questions by Mr. MacDonald that someone had put the mosque on fire, and apart from that not much more is there. The witness has explained that there are various potential causes of fire, lightning or whatever other cause, and that the perpetrators were never identified. That seems to be the situation. And Mr. MacDonald has not -- I think not presented any evidence which contradicts or challenges this uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, but the Prosecution's case as presented is that mosques were intentionally torched as a policy, and I'm suggesting that the reaction of the municipality goes counter to that, and that's why I'm leading this evidence, to counter any inference from the Prosecution leading this information that this mosque was intentionally torched as part of an official policy of the people that were in power in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. MacDonald, was that underlying your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, there certainly is an aspect of the Prosecution case that mosques were targeted, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the evidence here has as given by the witness does not show even that it was put on fire by anyone or -- because you didn't ask any further questions where the witness said I don't know whether persons are to be blamed for it or whether it's lightning or whether -- it's what caused the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution accepts the evidence of the witness as the mosque was on fire and that the perpetrators, if there were any, were unidentified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's nothing. Mr. Ivetic, so for this specific instance the Prosecution, more or less, concedes that the cause of fire has not been established, at least not through this witness, and also not that -- of course, if you don't even know that, of course you can't even find perpetrators because you don't know whether there are any perpetrators. That seems to be the present situation. If there's any further need specifically to deal with the matter, then please proceed but in the understanding of this situation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would then would go to my next point, but I see we're at the time for the break. I have approximately three to four questions. I leave it to Your Honours whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we left it last time in the hands of Mr. Mladic and I'm inclined to do the same now. Three to four questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe my client is asking for the break to be taken, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take the break now. And now I didn't misunderstand you and what is follow after the break, Mr. Ivetic, where I did misunderstand Mr. MacDonald. We take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we wait for the witness, I would ask that the two pages in the English and the one page in the -- pardon me, the two pages in the B/C/S that reflect General Mladic 's comments be included in what has now been marked as P6921 MFI. That according to my information should be pages 66 and 67 in the B/C/S and 83 through 84 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was not MFI'd yet but it was -- the number was reserved --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Reserved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for it. And then if you would include that in your A version of the 65 ter number, Mr. MacDonald, then we have the contextualisation which the Defence seeks and which is, of course, accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, at temporary transcript page 48 today, you were asked about paragraph 17 of your statement and the 22.000 Muslims and Croats that transferred through Srbac on their way to Croatia. The question I want to ask you is: Who organised or was involved in this transfer of persons to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: On the basis of an agreement of Mr. Sama Ruga [phoen], president of the ICRC, and the vice-president of Republika Srpska, Nikola Koljevic, Srbac Davor was the safest area and it was inaugurated as the place where Croats and Muslims would be reunified with their families because of what was happening in the Krajina. In 1995 when the Knin Krajina fell, when Knin fell, when that stampede of Serbs went towards Serbia through Banja Luka, et cetera, then Muslims and Croats were being reunited with their families, and then Srbac Davor was the most secure and safe place where people could cross over, and the authorities of Davor and the authorities of Srbac ensured their safety from different provocations in the meantime as they were travelling from one place to another. They didn't really want to have any kind of homeless people attacking them, looting, and so on. About 20.000 Croats crossed over to Croatia through Srbac and Davor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know of any Croats or Muslim families from Srbac that left during this time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No. From Srbac and Kobasi? Well, I know that the hodza personally came to see me. He's the religious leader of the Muslims, if I can put it that way. He wanted to go see his daughter in Croatia, and we made sure that he could do it in a safe way. Maybe there were two or three Croat families from Srbac itself. However, the 22.000 that were on the move were from different municipalities. I don't know. Croat municipalities. And then out there, towards the Krajina. I mean, from the Krajina, yes, the Knin Krajina, Glamoc, Grahovo. Towards Banja Luka, Mrkonjic, around Gradiska, these Muslim and Croat villages. Many spent the night in Srbac. They couldn't be transported on that day because approval had to be given for each and every family from the Croat authorities. In order for them to be able to cross over into Croatia, they had to prove that they had someone in Croatia. It's a painstaking procedure, a tortured procedure. It went on for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned -- I believe you used the word "stampede" of Serbs leaving Knin. During that time-period were there persons known to you who left Srbac and were of non-Serb ethnicity who were worried about the influx of these refugees from Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: In Kobas, in Srbac, in Crnaja, Povelic there were non-Serbs who had agreed to cross over to Croatia briefly until things are arranged. Non-Serbs from the municipalities that we mentioned. I cannot identify them individually. This was dramatic dynamics, painful, emotional. For example, the Croat authorities would allow one spouse to cross over and not the other one, and then there would be a drama, and then we'd have to keep them in Srbac until their papers were in order. The municipality really exhibited something that we were commended for later on. People who had crossed over. I have to say that from Banja Luka the wife of a Serb soldier had left with these refugees. They were saying that she should be frightened, run away, not with Croats. She went back to Banja Luka. It was a stampede. People were so afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm totally lost why in the statement, when the 22.000 persons are mentioned in paragraph 17, it says, "at the same time." Now all that precedes refers to, well, if there is any date it's 1992, and now I do understand from the answer that we are talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is, of course, is totally confusing me. If at paragraph 15 we are talking about 1992 and even 17, without any further time reference, we read "at the same time," then I'm really surprised to end up in 1995 where only in paragraph 18 reference is made to the period from 1992 to 1995. If you want us to understand all this, then take an approach which allows us to understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can see that the statement does not have the precise date nor the ethnicity of the people identified. I hope that we now have on the record that information. I had one more question and I have to scroll back up to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we now understand that the 22.000 persons transfer of the population from BiH to the Republic of Croatia, that that is all 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the time. All the time less. But this was that much. In July, August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. yes. Now, I also think I understood from your answers that these were refugees coming from the Krajina, Serb refugees coming from the Krajina region in Croatia? Or Croatian refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two types. Serbs went to Serbia through Srbac-Kobas-Derventa, towards the highway up there, Bijeljina, all of that; whereas, the Croats went through Srbac to Croatia. Croat refugees went to Srbac and Davor, whereas the Serb refugees continued through Kobasi towards Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this then covers two streams of refugees: Serb refugees coming from Croatia and moving on to Serbia, if I understand you well, and Croatian refugees coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina moving to Croatia. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, the reference to the population from BiH in paragraph 17 is not very clear because these are two entirely different groups of people. So, therefore, part of the confusion may have been removed. There's still some astonishment what is presented in paragraph 17 and how it is presented. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I wanted to ask you in response to one of my prior questions at page 74, line 17 and onwards, you said: "In Kobas, in Srbac, in Crnaja, Povelic, there were non-Serbs who had agreed to cross" --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Crnaja, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... there were non-Serbs who had agreed to cross over to Croatia briefly until things are arranged." How briefly? When did these people return, if they returned?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Some did not return. Some. Younger people. A smaller number. The rest mostly returned in 1995, Dayton. They went to their homes, their land. Some returned after ten or two or three days, and we had huge problems on account of that. Why are they leaving? Why are they coming back? Spies? You know how it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. On behalf of my client and the rest of my team I thank you for your answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That completes my re-direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we give an opportunity for further questions to the Prosecution, I have one question for you. Earlier it turned out that you had no direct knowledge of the number of non-Serbs that had left Srbac, where you said you knew about 60 persons, and then you later said 60 families, and then the statistics gave even --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Families, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, when I first raised the issue --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you didn't correct me at all, talking about persons, but you later said it's about families, but you had no knowledge about that. Where does your knowledge come exactly from that all those who had left had returned to their property? Could you tell us what the basis of that statement is, the basis of your knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Their houses? Refugees from Vozuca moved into their houses, Serbs from there, a number of them. Fifteen, twenty families, I don't know exactly. When Bosniak Muslims returned, they were moved out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a problem for the municipality, but I was no longer the number one person in the municipality. But new buildings were built and that was resolved and everybody returned to their homes that temporarily were taken over by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any documentation about this happening, that everyone finally returned to their own property?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: We had a Department for Refugees in Srbac, and I think that it was the first one in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina to complete its job. They had nothing else to do because everybody had returned. I think that that department worked for a year. And they actually had all these people return to their homes that they had left temporarily. Mr. Cvijanovic had nothing left to do. He moved onto another job because property had been returned 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So all the new construction immediately after the war was finished was completed in one year so as to allow all non-Serbs to return to their property. Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Maybe a bit more than a year. There is an entire neighbourhood of Serbs from Vozuca who were first staying in Bosniak houses and then later on through international organisations a settlement was built for them. This was very rapid construction. And it went on for about a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to be able to -- for the Chamber to assess the reliability of this portion of the evidence, if the parties would have any documentation on the return of property to non-Serbs that had left Srbac, the Chamber would like to be informed. I have no further questions. Any questions, Mr. MacDonald?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just one topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, I'd like to go back to this number 22.000 people who went from Srbac to Davor. I had understood you to confirm that all 22.000 were non-Serbs, Muslims or Croats primarily. Is that correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Via Davor, yes. But those who went on towards Serbia, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The 22.000 people, were they Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: And Croats. They were from the municipalities between Krajina, Knin, all the way to Banja Luka. They crossed over legally, they were reunited with their families until the end of the operations, and after it's finished they returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not the question. Were all these 22.000 Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any personal information about the reunification with the families which suggests that the families of the Muslims were already in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I heard it on the street. But as I said, I was no longer a president -- the president after 1997, and I learned that from people I met in the streets; my former pupils, their parents, et cetera. But Srbac is a very unique example and a very positive example, even though there were incidents that we mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I -- I therefore do understand that whether they were reunified with their families is just something you heard in the streets and you have no personal knowledge about at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used to see and I still see people involved in legislature and judicial systems. People are coming from Kobas and working in cafe. If you go to Kobas, you see a new mosque. People approach me to greet me. These are unofficial manifestations, though, but as a person, this is a kind of proof to me that we were not that evil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you said the transfer of the 22.000 people happened in 1995. You remained in your post until 1997. During -- during your time-period, when you have been in the municipal administration, did you receive any information to that -- in that respect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- about the -- about the reunification of these transferred people with their families.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kobas is the most outstanding example in that. If there was 60 families, most of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not talking -- sorry, I'm not talking about Kobas and 60 people or families. I'm talking about the 22.000 transferred people. That happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, now I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That happened during your term of office. Did you receive any official information about the reunification of these people with their families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were just a point of transit. We were just in charge of ensuring their safe crossing over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally knew some people, but as for the others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further. Mr. Milincic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions, questions put to you by the parties, questions put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. It is Mr. Dusko Corokalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the -- well, the usher is -- has left the courtroom, so I hope that he'll bring the next witness with him upon return. Yes, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just two small housekeeping matter, Your Honour. I'm informed by my colleague that 65 ter number 13386A, which was provisionally marked as P06922, is now available in e-court. I would ask that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm very bad at numbers. Could you remind me of what this one was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: That is the second-last document we looked at. It is a Karadzic -- it is a transcript from the 24th -- sorry from the 14th Session of the RS Assembly in March 1992 and it is a speech of Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there's no need for further context pages, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On that one, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On that one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the cover page is included now. So then before you continue, I take it that you would like to have it admitted, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, P6922 is admitted into evidence. The next one, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: With regard to 65 ter number 02366A, I know that my friend asked for further pages with regard to context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: From the transcript I saw he asked for pages 66 and 67. Unfortunately in the B/C/S, mine only goes to page 66. Just to flag that up for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This has to be resolved before we can decide any further on the matter. We'll not, at this moment, partially admit. Let's wait until this has been resolved and then we'll decide on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Corokalo. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Corokalo, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a counsel for -- is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. I would ask that you first state your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: My name is Dusko Corokalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask that we call up 65 ter number 1D01676 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to come up, two or three words were already sufficient for me, Mr. Corokalo, so fear that are you a quick speaker. Could you please try to slowly speak so that the interpreters have an opportunity to interpret what you say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we now have before us a statement. Could you tell us whose signature is on the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to the last page of the document in the B/C/S original, we see here another signature and a date. Could you tell us whose signature is visible on this page.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: This is also my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, after signing this statement, did you have a chance to review the same in the Serbian language to confirm if everything is correctly recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is everything correctly recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to ask you today questions arising out of the same facts as in your statement, would your answers to those questions today be the same, in substance, as in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have taken a solemn declaration today to tell the truth. Does that mean that we can conclude the answers as written in the statement are truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D01676 into evidence. There are no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you're playing from the second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours, and good afternoon to you. I have no objection to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1676 receives number D785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D785 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would read the public summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness, Dusko Corokalo, was a reserve second lieutenant in the command of the 6th Sana Brigade of the VRS. In March 1992, he personally saw armed Muslim formations of the Patriotic League and Green Berets. Representatives of the SDA, the HDZ, and SDS agreed in the municipal assembly to peacefully split Sanski Most and the SJB police into two parts. However, the Muslims attacked and took over the municipal building. After negotiations failed, the Serbs took back the building with no casualties on either side. He recalls a well armed company of the Muslim army located in the area of Golaja and that the inhabitants of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje were supplying this formation. Brigade Chief of Staff Brajic negotiated the transfer of this Muslim formation to Bihac with their weapons in exchange for captured Serb soldiers. There was an armed Muslim group in the central part of Sanski Most called Mahala, which fought against the Serbs. Until the arrival of Arkan in 1995, there were several neighbourhoods with more than 1.000 inhabitants of Muslim and Croat ethnicity in Sanski Most. Arkan and his men did harm to these non-Serbs and also arrested and mistreated Serb army members. That completes the public summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. We have five minutes left for your first questions. If you have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. I do. I'll try to make the most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at page 4 in both versions of your statement, I would like do discussion paragraph 13 with you. Sir, in this paragraph you describe the interviews which you conducted of able-bodied males from Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. Can you tell us what happened to the people after you finished interviewing them.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: I participated in the screening or the questioning of people because the logistics wanted to have certain number of people. I and another two co-workers of mine worked on that. We never left the room, and therefore I don't know what happened to them afterwards, where they went, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, chronologically speaking, what had happened before in this area prior to these interviews being taken?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO
utterances.text: Our task was to collect additional information on the basis of intelligence that we already had. There were some names, Muslim names mentioned, and we tried to get more information whether there were more people of that kind in the logistics and to find out whether there were any remaining armed formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You were asked what happened to the people after you had finished interviewing them. You said you didn't -- never left the room, so therefore you wouldn't know. But how did they leave the room? Were they escorted out, and if so by whom; or did you just say, Well, please go home and they left the room or the premises without any further supervision or escort.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. They would leave the room. During those two days, I don't know what happened with them afterwards and whether there were any subsequent interventions and what kind of interventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did they come to your interview room? Were they escorted in or did you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that somebody had escorted them. Somebody should have done that. I don't know the names of those people. Those were completely different people that had nothing to do with our task, and we were tasked with conducting interrogations. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, whether they were escorted out, you had no idea either, had you, or did you have an idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose. I suppose that since they were in some of the rooms in the school that they were sent back to these very same rooms again, but what happened next, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you assumed that there were escorted in and escorted out of the room which you never left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does "no" mean in this -- do you disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I mean, I never left the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you assumed that they were escorted in and escorted out, but you didn't know what happened after the door -- behind the doors from which they entered and by which they left. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, we are at the time. Witness, we will adjourn for the day and I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that's testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30, although tomorrow morning you'll find most likely only two Judges here instead of three. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day, and if I say "we resume," I'd say the hearing of the case will resume tomorrow, the 18th of November, 2014, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning. At least it's my expectations that my colleagues will decide that it's in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case, whereas I am not available tomorrow for urgent personal reasons. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of November, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.
